activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
story:
Theodore set his tray down at the far end of the table, the seat nobody ever fought over, and unwrapped his sandwich without looking toward the window side of the cafeteria where Eric usually sat. It had been eleven days since Eric had shown Theodore's practice recording to half the orchestra, the one where Theodore cracked on the high note three times, and the two of them had not spoken since. The cafeteria smelled like pizza and disinfectant, and someone's milk carton tipped over two tables away, and Theodore watched it spread toward a napkin dispenser as if it were the most interesting thing in the world.

He had told his mom on Sunday that he was done being angry. She had asked whether that meant he and Eric would be best friends again, and he had said no, not yet, and then had worried all night that he was doing it wrong. It felt like forgiving ought to come with a repair kit, like the friendship should snap back together the moment the resentment drained out. His mom had driven him to school that morning and he had almost asked her about it, but the bell rang.

Harriet slid in across from him and stole a chip, which was their usual greeting. "You're still hiding over here," she said.

"I'm not hiding. I like the quiet end."

"Uh-huh." She bit the chip and studied him. "You look like you're doing a science problem in your head."

He decided to speculate out loud, since Harriet was better at people than he was. "Okay, so. Say somebody says they've forgiven a friend. Does that mean they're friends again, exactly like before? Or can you be somewhere in between?"

Harriet chewed for a second. "My mom says those are two different things. Forgiving just means you let go of the resentment. Reconciling means you rebuild the relationship. You can do the first one without the second."

Theodore turned his milk carton in a slow circle. That would explain the strange in-between feeling, like being off the hook but not back on the team. "So it's allowed," he said. "To be there."

"Sounds allowed to me."

He tested the idea the way he'd test anything, one small step. He carried his tray past the window side, set it down across from Eric, and said, "The high note thing. I'm not mad about it anymore. I forgive you."

Eric's fork stopped halfway. "So we're good?"

"Good, but not back yet. Not exactly." Theodore sat. "I don't know how else to say it."

Eric looked at his tray, then out the window at the soccer field, where two sixth graders were arguing over an out-of-bounds call. "That's weird," he said finally. "But it's better than you hating me, so I'll take it."

They ate for a while without talking, and it was not comfortable exactly, but it was not terrible either. Theodore noticed it was gradual, the easiness coming back in small pieces, like frost melting off a car window one patch at a time. Near the end of lunch Eric asked what piece he was playing for the recital, and Theodore told him, and Eric said the second movement was the good one, which was a thing the old Eric would have said.

The irony was that the recording Eric had leaked had made Theodore practice harder than anything all year, and now the high note rang out clean every time. He didn't say that part out loud. He just stacked his tray, and on his way to the drop-off window he said, "Same seat tomorrow?"

"Same seat," Eric said, and raised his milk carton like a toast.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
story:
Elena taped the old phone to the pantry shelf at nine thirty on Tuesday night, angling its camera at the last slice of pizza like it was a nature documentary about one very doomed animal. For three mornings in a row the slice had vanished, foil folded neatly over nothing, and nobody in the house would confess. Her brother had shrugged. Her mom had said, "Maybe you ate it and forgot," which was insulting, because Elena never forgot pizza.

Her first guess had been her brother, since he had a history of midnight raids that included an entire birthday cake in March. But a guess was not the same thing, and she had learned that the hard way. Last year at the science fair, the judge, a retired teacher named Mr. Sow from two streets over, had leaned over her poster about plant growth and asked, "What result would prove your idea false?" She had nothing. She still remembered standing there, mouth open, while he said that the philosopher Karl Popper had argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea was scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong. She had lost the ribbon to a kid who grew mold on purpose.

So this time she built it properly. The phone's camera would act as a motion sensor, recording anything that moved in front of the pizza. She cleared a shelf to accommodate the phone and a power cord, and she wrote her prediction on the fridge whiteboard where her brother could not miss it: if my idea is right, the video shows him at 11 p.m. If the video shows Mom, or Dad, or the cat somehow opening foil with paws, my idea is wrong and I will say so. Her brother read it over her shoulder and said, "You're going to feel ridiculous." "That's the deal," Elena said. "Ridiculous is a small price."

At breakfast she watched the footage with the volume low. At 11:04 the kitchen lit up, and into the frame walked her mother, hair in a towel, eating the slice standing up in the light of the open fridge like some kind of neighborhood cryptid. Her brother appeared behind Elena and made a sound like a kettle. "You owe me an apology," he said. "You owe me a slice," Elena said, and her mother, arriving late with coffee, looked at the paused screen and said, "That towel is very unflattering." "That part's subjective," Elena told her. "The eating is on the record."

She did feel a little bad about the brother thing. She had accused him before checking anything, back in March, over the cake, and he had actually been innocent then too, since the cake had gone to her mother's book club. She kept the video anyway. That evening Mr. Sow was out trimming his hedge, and she called across the fence, "I found out what my result would have to be. Last year. To prove me wrong." He set down the shears. "And did anything prove you wrong this week?" "Yes," Elena said. "Eleven oh four. Kitchen. Towel." She held up the phone, pressed play, and turned the screen toward him.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
story:
Georgia had signed up for the neighborhood cleanup because her friend Ivory promised there would be doughnuts at the end, but when they arrived at the park pavilion on Saturday morning, the volunteer with the clipboard sent them down the street to the community food bank instead. "We have too many people picking up cups," the woman said. "They need hands."

Inside the food bank, Mr. Popal was stacking cans with a speed that suggested he had done this ten thousand times. "Perfect timing," he said. "The truck from the farm is coming, and it's not cans." Georgia and Ivory joined their classmate Teagan, who was already leaning on a pallet with a look that said she had been told the same thing. When the truck pulled in, the driver opened the back and there they were: hundreds of potatoes, still dusty from the field, filling the whole truck bed.

"They call it gleaning," the driver said as they started unloading. "Gathering crops left in fields after harvest." Teagan frowned at a potato as if it had personally wronged her. "So the farmer just leaves potatoes in the ground on purpose?" The driver shrugged. "Machine can't get them all. Groups send volunteers out to glean farms so the produce can come here." Georgia turned that over in her mind. The food bank shelves held mostly cans, but a potato was a whole different thing, and she found herself wondering how many were out there in fields right now, waiting.

She decided to test something. "If we're being systematic about it," she said, lining the potatoes up in rows on the pallet, "we can count what one crate holds and multiply." They counted: forty potatoes in a crate, six crates. Teagan did the math twice because she trusted nobody, and got two hundred forty. "That's a lot of mashed potatoes," Ivory said solemnly, and even Mr. Popal laughed from behind the cans.

Near the end of the morning, Mr. Popal told them he used to work for a corporation downtown before he decided to retire and come stack cans instead, which Ivory said was the most dramatic career change she had ever heard of. The food bank smelled like dust and cardboard, and through the window Georgia could see the cleanup crew coming back from the park, dragging bags.

Before they left, Georgia found the sign-up sheet by the door. There was a line at the bottom for the gleaning trip next Saturday, picking leftover potatoes at the farm, and she wrote her name at the top of it. Teagan leaned over her shoulder and said, "Save a spot."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
story:
Juliette had babysat her cousins before, so when Ms. Zhang asked her to watch the little one downstairs for the evening, she said yes without asking any questions. That was her first mistake. She settled into the living room with her phone, expecting a six-year-old who wanted cartoons and snacks. When Ms. Zhang left, Juliette heard a fussing sound from the playpen by the window and looked over to find a baby, maybe eight months old, staring back at her with watery eyes.

"You're not a six-year-old," Juliette said out loud, and the baby's face crumpled. She scooped him up, patted his back, and paced the carpet until his crying shrank to hiccups. A sticky note on the coffee table read: Bottles in the fridge, cereal in the cupboard, he naps around seven. Nothing else. Juliette formulated a plan: feed him, rock him, lay him down, then watch her show in peace. Simple.

The crying started again the moment the bottle was empty, and it did not stop. She jiggled him, sang to him, checked his diaper, which was fine. He rubbed his eyes with his fists and wailed louder, and the tranquil living room she had been promised in Ms. Zhang's text felt very far away. Then he gave a huge yawn mid-scream, and Juliette stopped pacing. He was exhausted. Something was stopping him from sleeping, and she could not see what it was.

She carried him toward the playpen and studied it. There was a crib in the corner too, and next to it a stack of fluffy blankets, a quilt, a soft pillow, and a plush rabbit the size of a loaf of bread. He was staring at the rabbit, reaching for it, whining. That had to be it, she decided. He wanted his bunny. She reached for the rabbit, then froze, because a folded page was wedged under the crib mattress, half hidden. She pulled it out with her free hand. It was a printed page, and at the top, underlined twice, it said: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys. This lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome.

"Backs," Juliette read again. Firm, flat, empty. The rabbit went back on the stack. She cleared the crib completely, laid him down gently on his back, and stepped away, holding her breath. He fussed for thirty seconds, then his eyes drifted shut like little curtains, and the room went quiet.

Juliette sank onto the couch, exhausted. Her phone buzzed: a message from her friend Linkin asking how the babysitting was going. She typed back that she had survived her first real emergency, then noticed a second note stuck to the inside of the front door, one she had somehow missed all evening. "Thank you so much," it read. "His older sister is at her dad's tonight, so it's just the baby." Juliette stared at it, then laughed until she had to wipe her eyes. "Six-year-old," she whispered to the sleeping baby. "You nearly had me."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations are true for every number, such as 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1), because both sides are the same expression written differently.
story:
The letter about the math camp scholarship had been sitting on the fridge for a week, held up by a magnet shaped like a lemon. Gabrielle needed an A on Friday's test to qualify, and the test was on solving linear equations, which meant she needed to understand them by tonight. She had invited Keon over because he was the only person in her class who did the homework for fun, and now the two of them sat at the kitchen table with a bag of pretzels between them and a page of problems that smelled faintly of pencil shavings.

"Okay, watch," Keon said, chewing. "You do the same thing to both sides. It's like a seesaw. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other, so it stays balanced." He tapped the paper with his pencil, which had teeth marks all along the yellow paint.

Gabrielle worked through a few and it started to feel good, the way undoing a knot feels good. Then she hit a problem that looked almost sinister in its trickiness: 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1). She distributed the 2 on the right side, subtracted 2x from both sides, and stared at what was left. "Keon. Something's wrong. The x's are gone. It just says 2 = 2."

Keon leaned over, crunching a pretzel. "That's weird. Did we break it?"

She refused to believe the problem was broken. She decided to test it, the way her older sister tested whether the microwave was lying about popcorn times. "If it says 2 = 2, then any number I put in should work. Let's try one." She plugged in 5. Both sides came out to 12. She plugged in 0. Both sides came out to 2. She tried 100, and her pencil flew through the arithmetic. Both sides matched again.

"Every single one," she said slowly, and she could feel the idea settling into place, like a picture coming into focus. "The two sides are the same expression written differently. So it's true for every number. Not just some number. Every number."

"So what do you write as the answer?" Keon asked, dipping a pretzel into his juice, which was a habit she had decided to ignore.

"All real numbers, I think. And Ms. Lewandowski will know if I actually get it or if I just guessed." She flipped to the back of the book, found the answers, and ran her finger down the column. There it was, in tiny print: all real numbers.

She wrote the problem out again, cleanly, on a fresh sheet, and boxed the answer. "Friday," she said, and reached for another pretzel.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks.
story:
Gabrielle had promised her friends a poster by Saturday, and the poster had to be perfect, because Neriah and Marianne were coming over to vote by ballot on which of her three sketches would represent their group at the library contest. She sat at the kitchen table with a box of pencils and a blank sheet of Bristol board, and that was where the trouble started.

The first sketch needed a soft, dark sky, heavy with storm clouds, ominous enough that the little house at the bottom looked fragile. One pencil gave her exactly that. Then she picked up another pencil that looked the same size, same yellow paint, same sharpened point, and dragged it across the paper. The line came out pale and scratchy, like the sky was fading out of the picture. She tried the dark one again. Dark. The pale one again. Pale. "That's weird," she muttered, holding them side by side.

She turned the pencils in her fingers and found tiny letters stamped near the end. Different letters. She remembered her grandfather's desk drawer, full of old pencils, and the little chart he kept taped inside it, and suddenly the pieces fit together in her head. Pencil cores were made of graphite powder mixed with clay. If you added more clay, the pencil got harder and left lighter marks. So her pale pencil had more clay in it, and her dark one had less. That was a guess, though, and she wanted proof. She made a test strip, pressing both pencils as hard as she could. The pale one stayed pale even under her full weight, which was exactly what her idea predicted. She tried to refute it by switching hands, pressing lighter, pressing harder, but the pale line never got truly dark. Her guess held up.

The hard pencil wasn't useless, though. On the second sketch, a garden scene, she needed thin, light lines for stems and grass, and the hard pencil did that beautifully while the soft one blobbed everything into smudge. She finished all three sketches, one with a dark storm, one soft and hazy, one crisp and delicate, and taped them to the wall just as the doorbell rang.

Neriah and Marianne came in with a shoebox for the ballots, each of them writing one choice on a folded scrap of paper. Ms. Yamamoto from next door, who had come over to return a casserole dish, got to vote too, because Gabrielle decided three votes beat two. Gabrielle unfolded the papers one at a time. The garden won, two votes to one.

Neriah leaned close to the delicate grass blades. "How did you get lines this thin?"

Gabrielle held up the pale pencil. "More clay in this one," she said, and handed it over.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Desert rainfall is not just low but unreliable: a desert may go years with almost no rain and then get a heavy downpour in a single storm.
story:
The departure board flipped to DELAYED just as Savannah sat down at gate C12, and her mother sighed and went to buy coffee. Savannah pulled out her science homework, two climate graphs side by side. One showed a rainforest, with rainfall bars tall and steady every month. The other showed a desert, where the bars were so short they looked like a row of ants. She was supposed to compare them and she had written one sentence so far: the rainforest is wet and the desert is dry.

Nadine dropped into the next seat with her own worksheet. "I'm stuck too," she said. "Mr. Khoury gave us the graphs but my answer keeps saying the same thing. Wet, dry. Boring." Austen leaned over from across the aisle, holding up his phone. "Look at this. My grandma lives near a desert town and here's a photo from her street. There's a flood warning sign. A flood sign. In a desert. Why would anybody put that there?"

Savannah looked at the photo, then back at her graphs. The rainforest bars hardly changed from month to month, which made sense if floods were a worry there. But the desert graph showed something she had skipped past. Most of the rainfall bars were tiny, almost nothing, and then one single bar shot up taller than the rainforest bars beside it. She checked the year on the axis. Almost no rain for a long stretch, and then one enormous downpour in one single storm.

"That's the answer," she said. "It's not just that the desert gets less rain. It's unreliable. It can go years with almost nothing, and then one storm dumps a huge amount all at once." She pointed at the tall bar. "A rainforest gets its rain steadily. A desert gets it rarely, and all in a burst. So the ground and the plumbing in those towns can't handle a sudden storm, and the water invades the streets. That's why the sign is there."

Austen looked at his photo again. "So the sign isn't weird. It's the most sensible sign on the street." He typed a note to his grandma asking whether the town had ever flooded.

Nadine rewrote her answer on a fresh line, comparing the steady rainforest bars with the desert's empty years and one giant spike. Then she read it out loud. "The rainforest is predictable. The desert is not, and that's the point." Savannah wrote her own final sentence in her neatest printing, then turned the worksheet upside down on her lap and closed her eyes to wait for the boarding call. Somewhere down the concourse, a voice announced that Flight 472 would begin boarding in twenty minutes.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars; maggots grew in open jars, but not in jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat.
story:
Matteo's project sat on table six, between Nadine's homemade lava lamp and a drone with a broken propeller that Quinn kept picking up and spinning like it might fix itself. Matteo's own display was simpler: two jars, one banana in each, and a sign that said WHERE DO FRUIT FLIES COME FROM? He had started the whole thing at home, when his little sister insisted that rotting fruit made flies all by itself. Matteo didn't believe it, but he couldn't prove her wrong, and that bothered him for two whole weeks.

He had tried, sort of. He covered one jar with gauze held on by a rubber band and left the other open on the windowsill. Then his mom made him move both jars to the garage, where a small fan clicked on and off to regulate the temperature, which was great for the jars and terrible for anyone trying to hear themselves think in there. Every day he counted the flies. Open jar: five, then nine, then too many to count without squinting. Gauze jar: zero. Always zero. He had guessed that would happen. He just hadn't known what to call the guess.

"Is that your question or your answer?" Mr. Aziz stopped at table six, holding a clipboard. He taught fifth grade science and judged the fair every year, and he had a way of asking questions that felt like traps and then turned out to be doors.

"Both?" Matteo said. "I mean, I guessed the flies wouldn't show up in the covered jar, and I was right, but my sister still says the fruit makes them."

Quinn leaned over from table seven, drone under one arm. "That's a hypothesis," he said. "A testable guess."

Mr. Aziz nodded slowly and didn't take the word away from him, which was how Matteo knew Quinn had actually gotten it right for once. "So what does your evidence tell you?"

Matteo looked at his jars. In the open one, tiny flies crawled on the banana like they owned it. In the gauze one, the banana was brown and soft and completely alone. Something was getting into the first jar and staying out of the second, and the gauze was the only difference. He hadn't seen it happen. He couldn't see it happen. But the pattern only made sense one way.

"That the flies come from outside," Matteo said. "They get to the fruit. The gauze blocks them, so no flies, even though the fruit rots just the same. My sister's version says flies should show up in both jars, and they didn't, so her version is wrong." He paused. "Politely wrong."

Mr. Aziz flipped a page on his clipboard. "You know someone did this exact experiment in 1668? Francesco Redi. He used meat instead of fruit. Maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the jars he covered with gauze that kept the flies off the meat."

"Did people believe him?" Matteo asked.

"Eventually," said Mr. Aziz. "It took a while. People liked the old idea." He moved on to Nadine's lava lamp, where the blobs were rising and sinking with metronome-like calm.

Matteo wrote Redi's name and date on his poster in marker, then stood back. Across the gym, his little sister stood with her arms crossed, defiant, studying the jars from a distance. Matteo waved her over and pointed at the gauze jar. "Look," he said. "Rotten banana. Zero flies. Want to count them again?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.
story:
The church smelled of candle wax and lilies, and Maria sat in the third pew between her mother and Esteban, who had come even though he barely knew her grandmother. On the altar, beside the conventional spray of white flowers, someone had placed Grandmother's blue cardigan, folded neatly over the rail. Maria kept her eyes on it because looking at the closed casket made her throat close.

Halfway through the service, Esteban leaned over and whispered that the soloist had just mimicked a car alarm outside, perfectly, two notes rising. Maria pressed her hand over her mouth, but the laugh escaped anyway, a short hiccup that echoed against the stone walls. The woman in front turned around. Esteban went red. Maria stared at the hymnal and thought she was the worst granddaughter alive, laughing six days after the funeral announcement had come.

She barely spoke at the reception in the basement. She watched Esteban eat three sandwiches. She watched Isra, who arrived late from swim practice, sign the memory book with the felt pen Grandmother had always kept by her phone. When Maria's mother finally sat down beside her with two paper cups of juice, Maria said, "I laughed. During the hymn. At Grandma's funeral. How could I do that?"

Her mother turned her cup slowly in her hands. "The week before yours, I laughed at a movie with your aunt," she said. "Then I cried in the parking lot. Grief researchers actually mapped this. In their 1999 dual process model, two researchers named Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life." She took a sip. "They're Dutch, I think. Or she is. Anyway, the back and forth is normal. It's not a betrayal."

"You laughed at a movie the same week?" Maria asked.

"Two days after, at the theater on Delmore Street," her mother said. "Ask your aunt if you don't believe me."

Maria thought about the last six days: crying at the breakfast table Monday, then helping her father fix the porch screen for an hour without thinking of anything. Sad at the hospital visiting hours, then arguing with Esteban about which soccer team was worse, laughing so hard her ribs hurt. Back and forth, like a tide, like the pendulum clock in Grandmother's hallway that swung even when nobody wound it.

The priest came by to say the family could view the flowers one last time before the evening service. Maria stood, smoothed her black skirt, and walked up the center aisle with her mother. At the rail she picked up the blue cardigan, held the wool to her face for a moment, then folded it over her arm to take home. "I'm going to wear it," she told her mother. "Tomorrow, to school."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: The Nicene Creed, recited in many Christian churches, ends by looking forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.
story:
Aubrey stood at a folding table in the gymnasium with her poster board balanced against her hip, watching the cultural festival crowd move between the booths. Her poster had two columns, one for Christianity and one for Buddhism, and the Buddhism side was full while the Christianity side had exactly one sentence in it. Mr. Sánchez had said every project needed at least one comparison nobody in class would expect, and she had promised him hers would be about what happens after death.

She had gotten her one sentence three weeks ago, at her grandmother's funeral. She could still hear the whole church standing up, everyone reciting the same words without looking at a book, and the last lines landing on her like a door opening somewhere far away: they looked forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. She had whispered to her mom afterward, "What does that even mean?" and her mom had said, "That's what we believe happens after we die," which was true but didn't tell her much. She'd felt embarrassed for asking, and she still wasn't sure she should have. Maybe some things were meant to stay vague.

River waved from the Buddhist association booth, where incense smoke curled up toward the gym ceiling. "You came! Did you bring your questions?"

"Only the big one." Aubrey set the poster on their table, next to a poster of a wheel with six sections. "You said in Buddhism people are reborn. So the dead come back as new people. That's not the same as resurrection, right? Resurrection means the actual dead rising, the same people, in a world to come after this one. That's what my grandmother's church says every Sunday. It's called the Nicene Creed, and those words are the end of it."

River nodded slowly. "Rebirth is more like a flame passing from one candle to another. Same fire, new candle. The wheel shows the realms you can be born into." River pointed at one section, then made a face. "Some of these realms have hungry ghosts in them. They have huge stomachs and tiny throats, so they can never get full. Kind of predatory, the way wanting works in the story, always grasping for more."

Aubrey wrote fast. Then she stopped, tapping her pen. "Here's my problem. Nobody can check either one. You can't watch someone die and then come back and report. So how do I compare two things that might both be, like, an illusion of certainty?" She tested the idea out loud, half expecting River to argue. "Maybe I compare what the beliefs do, not what they claim. Like, my grandmother believed she'd see my grandpa again, and it made her less afraid. Does rebirth do that too?"

River was quiet for a moment, straightening the incense sticks. "My grandma says the hungry ghost story isn't about after death at all, not really. It's about how we live now, always hungry for stuff." River looked up. "Maybe that's your answer. Both stories are about now, and afterward."

Aubrey chewed her pen and looked at her lopsided columns. She thought about boycotting the whole comparison and just painting the two posters side by side, letting people see them without a verdict. Then she wrote in the middle of the poster, between the columns, "Both look forward."

Behind her, Mr. Sánchez leaned over her shoulder and read it. "Say that part again out loud to me, the creed ending."

"We look for the resurrection of the dead," Aubrey said, "and the life of the world to come."

"That's it exactly," he said, and tapped the center of her poster twice.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: When smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds.
story:
Ruby sat in the dentist's waiting room holding a pamphlet about tobacco, because the only other reading choices were a fishing magazine from 2019 and a poster about flossing that said "Plaque Attack!" in cartoon letters. She had a science presentation on Friday and her topic was how nicotine tricks the brain, and so far all she had was a diagram with too many arrows.

Across from her, a girl about sixteen was tapping her foot and checking her phone. A boy named Nolan from Ruby's class was there too, holding his jaw and saying very little. Yan had come along for moral support and was reading over Ruby's shoulder.

"My uncle does this thing," the older girl said, mostly to the ceiling. "The second anything goes wrong, he's reaching for a cigarette. Stress hits, cigarette. Bad phone call, cigarette. Why is it that fast? It's like his hand knows before he does."

Ruby looked down at her pamphlet. Under a heading called "Speed of Delivery" it said that when smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds. She read it twice. Ten seconds. That was faster than Yan could find a pencil.

"That's the answer," Ruby said. "It's not that his hand knows first. It's that when he inhales, the nicotine gets to his brain in about 10 seconds. So the relief shows up almost instantly, and his brain links the cigarette to feeling better, right away. Faster than almost anything else he could do."

"That's the reward pathway?" the girl asked.

"Yeah. The brain has this system that repeats whatever pays off fast. Nicotine pays off in 10 seconds, so the brain keeps nominating cigarettes as the solution to everything."

Ms. Fitzgerald, Ruby's neighbour, was in the next chair getting a filling and could apparently hear everything through the open door. "Did you just say nicotine hits the brain in 10 seconds?" she called, voice muffled by the dentist's tools.

"When smoke is inhaled, yes," Ruby said. "It's in the pamphlet."

"Well, that's the most useful thing anyone's said in this office all week."

The girl had stopped tapping her foot. "So my uncle basically has a 10-second reward machine wired to a paper tube of leaves."

"That's logical," Yan said. "Also gross."

"Also gross," Ruby agreed. She flipped the pamphlet over and found a diagram of the brain's reward pathway, clean and simple, with the word dopamine circled in red. She held it up so the girl could see it.

"Keep it," the girl said. "I'm going to show my uncle. Then I'm going to hide his lighter."

The hygienist opened the door and said, "Nolan, you're up." Nolan stood, still holding his jaw, and pointed at Ruby's diagram on his way past.

"Use that one," he said. "The arrows actually make sense."

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: A screener must be standing still when contact is made; moving into the defender is an offensive foul called a moving screen.
story:
Ethan stood at the top of the key in the park's cracked asphalt court, bouncing the ball so hard it sounded like a drum. Gabryel was supposed to cut toward the hoop, but he kept drifting off toward the fence like a pigeon looking for fries.

"Pick and roll," Ethan called, tapping his hip the way the real point guards did on TV. "Gabryel, set the pick right here, then roll to the basket."

Gabryel jogged over and planted himself near the defender, Miley's little brother, who was guarding Ethan like his life depended on it. Ethan started his drive, and Gabryel, eager to help, took one big step sideways and bumped the kid with his whole shoulder. The kid went down like a bowling pin and howled loud enough to make a woman walking three dogs stop and stare.

"Offensive foul," announced Miley from the sideline, sounding way too pleased about it. She was keeping score and had appointed herself referee for the afternoon. "That's a moving screen."

"A what?" Gabryel helped the kid up and dusted him off.

"A moving screen," Miley repeated. "The screener has to be standing still when contact happens. If you step into the defender, it's a foul."

Ethan chewed on that while he jogged back. So that was why his team always lost the ball whenever Gabryel tried to "help." It wasn't bad luck. It was a rule with a name, and Gabryel had been breaking it every single time, probably since the dinosaur era, back when the dinosaurs went extinct from watching him play. Ethan decided not to say that part out loud, mostly because Gabryel was bigger than him.

"Okay, new plan," Ethan said, spinning the ball on one finger, which immediately wobbled and fell. He picked it up like he'd meant to do that. "Gabryel, get to your spot and freeze. Feet planted like you're a fence post. Agriculture frozen. Whatever. Don't move a muscle until I've already gone past you. Then roll."

"I'm not a fence post," Gabryel said. "Fence posts can't do this." He attempted a spin move and nearly fell over.

"Which is why you're better than a fence post. Barely."

They ran it again. Gabryel set up on Ethan's left and froze so completely that a fly landed on his nose and he refused to swat it. Ethan's defender crashed into the stationary wall of Gabryel, bounced off, and Ethan slipped past, drew the other defender, then flipped the ball behind his back to Gabryel rolling to the rim. The layup clanked off the back of the rim, off the fence, and somehow dropped through.

The kid tried to dismiss the whole thing by claiming the fence counted as goaltending, but Miley just wrote two on the scoreboard in chalk.

"One more," Ethan said, wiping sweat off his forehead with the bottom of his shirt. "Same play. Gabryel, freeze."

"Fly and all," Gabryel said, holding out his arms like a scarecrow. "Watch me not move."

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: If a company fails completely, its stock price can fall to zero, so a stockholder can lose every dollar they put in.
story:
Violet slid three dollars across the table for a bag of honeycrisp apples and watched the man count her change. That was her whole job this morning, helping Ms. Addo work her stall at the farmers' market, and she took it seriously, because Ms. Addo had promised to pay her twenty dollars at the end of the day. Twenty real dollars, which Violet intended to invest, the moment she figured out what investing actually meant.

"Your apple guy," said Alexandria, appearing beside her with a cup of cider. "My mom said the crafts table has a carved sailboat with an authentic hand-painted hull, and I want to see it before Mikhail gets here. He's in a mood."

Mikhail was in a mood. When he arrived, he was carrying a jar of pickles he didn't want and a phone he wouldn't put down. Last spring, Violet remembered, he had stood on the bleachers waving his arms and announcing to everyone that he'd put every dollar of his birthday money into one company everyone online was yelling about. "It's basically guaranteed," he'd said then. This morning he set the pickles on the stall edge and said, "It went to zero."

"Zero zero?" Violet asked.

"The whole thing fell apart," Mikhail said. "Every dollar I put in, gone. The stock price just went to zero, because the company failed completely." He shrugged, but his voice had a hole in it.

Violet handed him an apple without asking, because that seemed like the thing to do, and Ms. Addo, who had been weighing tomatoes, quietly added a second one to his hand.

"So that's the answer," Violet said slowly, working it out on the spot. "My dad's been going on about stocks and bonds and I didn't get the difference. But if a stock can go to zero like that, then a stock is riskier. With a bond, the company owes you money, it promised to pay you back. It's like..." She looked around the market. "It's like the vendors here. Ms. Addo signed a contract with the market manager, so the market has to give her a spot and she has to pay the fee. Nobody can just wave a magic wand and make it zero."

"Except I did," Mikhail said. "I waved my own magic wand. It was called putting everything in one basket."

"That's not what it was called," Alexandria said. "It was called a birthday."

Mikhail laughed, finally, a real one. Ms. Addo slipped him a bag of grape tomatoes and said the first customer of the day who actually listened to her tomato advice always got a bonus.

"So you're splitting it up," Violet said. "When you get money again. Some in a bond, because it's a promise, and some in a stock, and never all of it in one place." She counted her apple money again. "Twenty dollars at the end of today, split two ways."

"Three ways," Alexandria said. "I want in on your plan. But first, the boat."

They walked together past the cider press and the beekeeper, and Violet pointed at the crafts table. "There's your authentic hull," she said, and Mikhail was already reaching for his pickle jar to trade.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
story:
Livia set the cutting board on the counter and lined up three onions like pale planets. Tonight she was making soup for the whole family, the first real dinner she had cooked alone, and she wanted everything to go right before her parents got home at six. She peeled the first onion, cut it in half, and started chopping. Within thirty seconds her eyes were stinging and tears ran down her cheeks.

"Great," she said out loud, wiping her face with her sleeve. "I look like I'm crying over soup."

She remembered a text Rosalie had sent her last week from her own kitchen. Rosalie had written, "Help, I'm making chili and the onions are making me cry, I'm not even sad!!" Under it she had typed, "I looked it up. Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that make a gas. The gas floats up into your eyes. That's it. A vegetable crime." Livia had laughed at the time and written back a single onion emoji. Now she read the message again, standing at the counter with her phone in one wet hand.

If the gas floated upward from the cut cells, she reasoned, then the problem was the space between the onion and her eyes. So she tried a test. She pulled her swim goggles from the hook by the back door, snapped them on, and chopped the second onion. Nothing. Her eyes stayed dry. She looked ridiculous, but it worked. Then she tried the third onion without goggles, holding her breath and leaning far back, and that failed completely, which told her the gas reached her eyes no matter how she angled her face. Only blocking her eyes had stopped it.

Ms. Okonkwo's voice came back to her from the community cooking class last fall. "A pot of soup is a bit of a paradox," she had said, stirring a big pot while Livia and Kolby peeled carrots beside her. "The ingredient that hurts you going in is the one that makes everything taste better by the end." Livia hadn't understood then. Now she slid all those tear-causing onions into the pot with butter, and slowly the kitchen filled with a sweet, golden smell as they softened and went brown at the edges.

She stirred, added broth, and checked the clock. Her mother walked in at ten to six, sniffed the air, and frowned at the goggles lying on the counter.

"Swimming before dinner?" her mother asked.

"Onion defense system," Livia said. "Want to try them? There's a second pair by the door."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: The formula =SUM(B2:B10) adds every cell from B2 to B10; the colon between the two cells marks a range.
story:
Wyatt had agreed to help at Mr. Barrett's phone repair shop every afternoon for one week, and in exchange Mr. Barrett would fix his cracked screen for free. So far the work consisted of sorting screws into trays and holding a flashlight while Mr. Barrett wrestled a battery out of a tablet that had been swimming in a puddle. Then, on Thursday, Mr. Barrett pointed at the ancient computer behind the counter.

"Week's till receipts, all on paper," he said. "Type them into that spreadsheet program and tell me what we took in." He shut off the water valve to the ultrasonic cleaner, wiped his hands, and disappeared under the sink with a wrench.

Wyatt opened the program and made a column, B2 through B10, one day's morning sales, afternoon sales, and the five mysterious rows labeled "misc." He knew one way to add: he typed =B2+B3+B4+B5+B6+B7+B8+B9+B10. It worked, but it looked like a snake that had swallowed a keyboard, and if he ever added a row he would have to redo the whole thing. Kyla, who had come in to buy a charger and stayed to watch, leaned over his shoulder.

"My mom does these," she said. "Try equals, SUM, open parenthesis, B2, colon, B10." Wyatt typed =SUM(B2:B10). The same total appeared, instantly, in one short line. He stared at the colon, the smallest mark on the screen, doing the work of eight plus signs. The long version and the short one gave the equivalent answer, but one of them was a machine and the other was a confession of defeat.

He had to be sure, though. He deleted it and tried =SUM(B2,B10), with a comma. That gave a much smaller number, just the first day plus the last one, as if Wednesday had never happened. He put the colon back and the full total returned. So the comma picked only those two cells, and the colon meant everything from here to there. "The colon marks a range," Kyla said, in the tone of someone reciting her mother.

"There's our week," Wyatt said, and clicked the chart button. The numbers transformed into a row of bars, and one bar, Wednesday afternoon, towered over the rest like it had something to prove. Mr. Barrett surfaced from under the sink, still holding the wrench, and squinted at it.

"What happened Wednesday afternoon?"

"That's when the sprinkler by the bus stop broke," Wyatt said. "Half the neighborhood came in with dead phones."

Mr. Barrett looked at the bar chart, then at the valve in his hand, then out the window toward the bus stop, and did not say anything at all.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Glasses for astigmatism use cylindrical lenses, which bend light more in one direction than in the other.
story:
Victoria got her glasses on a Tuesday, and by lunch she was on the playground turning them sideways to see what would happen. The frames belonged to her now, even though her mom had complained about the expense twice on the drive home, and the world through them was suddenly sharp in a way she had not known it was blurry. Trees had individual leaves. The basketball net had actual netting.

"Stop spinning them, you'll scratch them," Nelia said, but Victoria wasn't spinning them. She was rotating them slowly, one finger on the corner of the frame, and something strange was happening. When she turned the lens sideways, the net stretched. It got taller and thinner, like taffy being pulled, then squashed back the moment she turned the glasses straight again. She tried it on the hopscotch grid, on the door of the gym, on her own hand. Everything stretched one way and squashed the other. Was it always the same direction? She lined the glasses up with the painted line of the four-square court and watched it stretch along its length, then thicken when she rotated ninety degrees.

Alma came over and accused her of breaking them already. "I'm not breaking them," Victoria said. "I'm testing them." She held the glasses up so Alma could look through while Victoria turned them, and Alma saw it too, the chain-link fence warping like reflections in a funhouse mirror. Why would a lens do that? Her old magnifying glass at home had never stretched anything, and she wondered what made this one different.

She remembered the word on the paper from the eye doctor's office. Astigmatism. Her lenses, the paper said, were cylindrical lenses. When she got home she would look up why that word mattered, but here on the playground she could already guess at the rule: a lens that was curved like a cylinder, tall in one direction and flat in the other, might bend light more in one direction than in the other. That would explain everything. The glasses only fixed her eyes when they sat exactly right on her face, because the stretching direction had to match her eyes' own stretching direction. If she rotated the glasses, the stretch went the wrong way and the whole picture warped. So the frames were not just holding the lenses. They were aiming them.

Mr. Nkosi, who taught science, was crossing the playground on duty, and Victoria called out a question that was really half an answer. "If a lens bends light more one way than the other, does that mean it only works in one position?" He smiled and said, "Cylindrical lenses, yes. You've noticed that already, have you?" She had. She put the glasses back on, straight and careful, and looked at the four-square court, where the lines sat still and true.

"Alma," she said, "stand over there by the fence and wave your left hand."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
The lobby filled slowly, avatars drifting in and arranging themselves in two symmetrical rows, red team on one side, blue on the other. Georgia was adjusting her loadout when Nihal's message scrolled up the side panel, the one everyone in the lobby could see. Then came a screenshot, and her stomach dropped before her brain even caught up, because the screenshot was of her words. Her actual words, from a private chat two nights ago: "Sarah-Maude hogs the sniper rifle every single match and I'm so tired of it."

"Lobby chat is public," her mom liked to remind her, meaning don't type anything a stranger couldn't read. Georgia had followed that rule. She had kept the complaint out of the lobby, out of the team channel, and sent it privately to exactly one person, someone she had trusted since fourth grade. Now here it was, pasted into a chat with thirty people in it, and Sarah-Maude was in this lobby. Sarah-Maude's avatar stood frozen at the top of the blue row, not moving, which meant she was reading.

Georgia typed nothing. She had learned enough about this game's economy of information, who traded screenshots like rare drops, to know that reacting in public would only sustain the drama longer. Instead she opened a private window, but this time she thought first. A private message was only as private as the person who received it. That was the real rule, she realized, and she had never once tested it.

She sent a single line to Nihal, the one other person who might know where the screenshot came from: "Who posted that?" Then she waited, watching the countdown tick from thirty, her thumbs hovering. In the lobby, Sarah-Maude finally moved, rotating her avatar until it faced Georgia's, pixel eyes locked across the divide. The match could not start while someone stayed unready, and Sarah-Maude was not clicking ready.

Nihal's answer arrived at fifteen seconds. "I sent it to Priya's cousin as a joke. I didn't know she was in this lobby." So that was the chain: Georgia to Nihal, Nihal to someone else, someone else to thirty people. The screenshot had traveled like a dropped coin, passed from hand to hand, and every hand had been able to copy it.

Georgia took a breath. There were ten seconds left, and the whole lobby was waiting. She typed into the public channel, where everyone could see it, on purpose this time: "Sarah-Maude, I said that. I'm sorry. Can we talk after the match?"

Sarah-Maude's avatar tilted, once, like a nod. Then she clicked ready, and the doors opened.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
The poster had been blank for three days, and Mr. Katz was losing patience. Every student group in the school was supposed to generate a display for the heritage fair by Friday, and the student council board outside the gym still showed nothing but a few pencil marks and a dried smear of glue that Livia thought looked like a fungus spreading across the paper.

"That's it," Livia said, dropping her backpack on the floor. "We're putting up a board about who we all are. Names, flags, one sentence each. Simple."

Cedric picked at the corner of the blank poster paper and said nothing, which was strange, because Cedric always had an opinion about everything, including cafeteria pizza. David, who was already sketching an approximate map of his grandfather's village in blue marker, looked up.

"What?" David said. "Cedric, you in?"

"I don't know what I'd even write," Cedric said.

"You're from here," David said. "That's easy."

"That's not the same thing as being nothing," Cedric said, and walked off down the hall.

Livia stared at the swinging door. David shrugged and went back to his map, but Livia couldn't shrug it off. She had known Cedric since fourth grade. She thought about the way he never came to the international food day, and the way his grandmother picked him up sometimes speaking a language Livia couldn't place, and how Cedric always switched topics when anyone asked where his family was from. There was something underneath his answer, and she wanted to know the rule for it. Not just for the poster. She wanted to know who actually got to say what a person is.

After school she went to the library computer and typed question after question, refining her search until the words on the screen finally matched what she was hunting for. She found a document with a long name, adopted on 13 September 2007 by the United Nations: the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. She scrolled, and one line stopped her cold. It said Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership. She read it twice, then copied it into her notebook, word for word.

She found Cedric the next morning at his locker, before the hallway got loud. "I looked something up," she said. "The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007. It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership." She held up her notebook. "So nobody else decides. Not David, not the poster, not me."

Cedric closed his locker slowly. For a long moment he just looked at the page, and Livia could hear the clock above the door ticking.

"My grandma's Cree," he said finally. "I never wrote it down anywhere before because I thought somebody would tell me I was doing it wrong."

"Then write it however you're doing it," Livia said, and handed him the marker.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
The living room smelled like popcorn and salsa, and every seat was taken. Ruby sat on the floor between Bo and Rami, her eyes glued to the screen where the World Cup match was tied with twenty minutes left. On the couch, her cousin, who was visiting from England, kept jumping up every time the crowd in the stadium did the wave.

When the whole stadium rippled again, the cousin shouted, "Look, a Mexican wave!" Bo frowned. "It's just the wave," he said. "That's what everybody calls it." The cousin shook her head. "In England we call it the Mexican wave. Always have." Rami laughed. "That's weird. Why would it be Mexican?" The cousin shrugged and went back to the game, but Ruby could not let it go. Two names for the same thing meant there had to be a reason, and she wanted to find it.

She pulled out her tablet and started searching while the crowd roared on without her. Bo leaned over. "You're missing the best part." "I'm doing science," Ruby said. "There are two names, so one of them had to come from somewhere. If I can find where the wave got famous, maybe I'll find the name." Her searching was slow and a bit meticulous at first, too careful, until she learned to just skim for the big words that repeated.

The popcorn bowl emptied fast, and it seemed to evaporate within minutes because everyone kept grabbing handfuls during the tense plays. Ruby barely noticed. She had found something. She read it twice, then stood up in front of the TV during a lull in the action.

"Okay, listen," she said. "The wave became known worldwide at the 1986 World Cup. In Mexico." Rami sat up straight. "That's why your cousin calls it the Mexican wave?" "I think so," Ruby said. "The whole world saw it there, so a lot of English speakers outside North America got the name from that." Bo looked unsure. "But how do we know that's really it? Maybe the name just happened anyway." Ruby liked that he was pushing back, because it meant she needed to test it.

"Think about it like this," she said, pacing between the couch and the TV. "It's like a neuron passing a signal. The wave didn't stay in Mexico. It jumped from one crowd to another, all around the world, and the name jumped with it, at least in some places. Bo, you and I got the shorter name, so the signal reached us different." The cousin grinned. "She's good, this one."

Mr. Costa, the neighbour who had let himself in when he heard the cheering, raised his soda can. "To the wave, whatever you call it." Then the stadium crowd stood up again, section by section, a giant ring rolling around the bowl, and Rami pointed at the screen. "There goes your neuron, Ruby. Look at it go."

Ruby turned just in time to see the last section rise, the wave sweep past the camera, and the whole room, without anyone deciding to, stood up in one motion and threw their arms overhead.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A timekeeper watches how long each agenda item takes, so one topic does not use up the time planned for the others.
story:
The Maplewood Neighborhood Kids' Club had failed to reach the last item on its agenda three meetings in a row, and Ruby, the new president, had promised her mom it wouldn't happen again. She spread the agenda across the kitchen table: pond cleanup, bake sale money, and last, the nature walk. The nature walk was the item Krish cared about most, and every time it got skipped, he dragged his backpack to the door without saying goodnight.

"Maybe you should just put the walk first," her mom suggested, drying a plate.

"Then something else gets skipped," Ruby said. She stared at the paper. The problem wasn't the order of the words. Something invisible was eating the time, and she couldn't see what. At the last meeting, they had talked about the bake sale for what felt like ten minutes and somehow forty had gone by. She decided to run a practice meeting at home, with her little brother and two chairs standing in for Krish and Auston, and she would test one idea: somebody would watch the clock.

On Saturday, the real meeting started in Ruby's garage. Krish arrived first, then Auston, then the twins from down the street. Ruby read the agenda aloud and added a new job before anything else. "Krish, you're the timekeeper," she said. "You watch how long each agenda item takes, so one topic doesn't use up the time planned for the others."

Krush sat up straighter, buoyant with importance, timer in hand. The pond cleanup got fifteen minutes, and when the twins started arguing about whose idea the bake sale had been, Krish held up the timer without a word and pointed at the numbers. Auston laughed. They wrapped up the bake sale in twelve minutes flat, and when Krish called out that item two was done, Ruby still had eleven minutes left for the walk.

They planned the whole route, past the creek and the hill where ferns thrived in the damp shade. Krish read them a stanza from a poem about ferns he'd found in a library book, and Auston said it rhymed wrong, and Krish said that was the point.

Walking home later, Ruby turned the afternoon over in her mind. Part of her wondered whether she should have tried the timekeeper idea weeks ago, before Krish stopped saying goodnight. He might have stayed mad anyway. She had no way of knowing, and she decided she could live with that. At the corner he caught up to her, backpack bouncing.

"Same job next meeting?" he asked. "I liked being the timekeeper."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Checking in privately afterward with a classmate who was teased, and telling them it was not okay, can help them feel less alone even if nobody stepped in at the time.
story:
Lincoln sat at the kitchen table pretending to do his math homework while the argument replayed in his head. At lunch yesterday, some kids had circled Cassius and made jokes about his secondhand shoes, calling them counterfeit sneakers like it was the funniest thing in the world. Cassius had laughed along, but his ears went red, and Lincoln had just sat there, frozen, staring at his tray like it contained something fascinating. Now the numbers on his worksheet blurred, and he kept thinking about the way nobody had said a word. Even Kierra, who usually spoke up about everything, had been quiet.

"You've read that same problem four times," his mother said, setting a glass of milk beside him. "That's not how homework works."

"I know." He tapped his pencil against the table. "If somebody gets teased and everyone just watches, does the person think everyone agreed with it? Like, silence kind of sounds like a yes?"

His mother pulled out the chair across from him. "Sometimes it does. Why, what happened?"

He told her about the shoes, about freezing. She didn't lecture him, which he was grateful for, because he was already doing enough of that himself. Instead she asked, "Is Cassius someone who'd rather be left alone with it, or someone who'd want to know you didn't think it was funny?" That was the question, Lincoln realized. He'd been so busy thinking about what he should have said in the cafeteria that he hadn't thought about Cassius at all, about what Cassius might be carrying around since yesterday.

He picked up his phone, then put it down. A text felt too small for this. He texted one thing instead: can I come over for a bit? Cassius replied in under a minute, which told Lincoln something too, since Cassius usually took hours, like he was some giant corporation with a whole department for answering messages.

Cassius's house was two streets over. His little sister let Lincoln in, and Cassius was at the kitchen counter building a model car, one wheel half attached. "My dad got me this," Cassius said, like he was heading off the shoe subject before it arrived. "It's supposed to accelerate from zero to crazy fast when you let it go."

"It's cool," Lincoln said. He sat down, watched the wheel spin loose for a second, and then made himself say it. "That stuff at lunch yesterday. It wasn't funny. I should have said something, and I didn't, but I thought you should know I didn't think it was okay."

Cassius kept his eyes on the car, but his shoulders came down a little. "Nobody said anything," he said. "I figured everybody agreed with them."

"Nobody agreed. Everybody just wimped out. Including me."

Cassius snapped the wheel into place and set the car on the floor. He pulled back the little motor, held it, and glanced up. "Want to race it down the hallway?"

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Parallel lines like railway tracks or the two edges of a road look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet.
story:
Norah's street drawing looked like a pile of boxes that had lost a fight with a rake. She leaned over the table at the community art studio, glaring at it, while Kaelyn sharpened a pencil on the other side of the room.

"You're supposed to make all the lines run toward one spot," said Finnegan, who was drawing next to her with the confidence of someone whose street actually looked like a street. "Ms. Weber called it the vanishing point."

"A point that vanishes," Norah said. "Great. The one part of this drawing that's invisible is the most important part."

"That's not what vanish means," Finnegan said, grinning. "A carnivore vanishing would be a lion disappearing. A point vanishing is just where the lines seem to go."

Norah flicked her eraser at him. She was still stuck on one thing, though: why did the lines have to run together at all? On a real street, the two edges of the road were the same distance apart the whole way. She knew that, because last summer she and her cousin had painted a hopscotch grid along the curb for the whole block, and every square had fit the same width of sidewalk. So why should a drawing of that street have its road lines squeezing together like a closing suitcase?

She thought about the footbridge over the train tracks behind the studio. "Come on," she told Finnegan, and they got permission from Ms. Weber, who was helping Kaelyn tape down a wobbly easel and only said, "Back in ten minutes, and don't drop anything on the tracks."

From the bridge, the rails ran out ahead of them toward the horizon, and Norah pointed. "Look. They meet. Right there."

"They get closer," Finnegan argued. "They don't meet. Tracks that met would derail every train in the country."

"Walk out there and check," Norah said.

"I'm not walking on the tracks, Norah."

"Fine. Watch, then." A freight train rattled under the bridge, and as it accelerated away down the line, the cars stayed the same width over the rails, wheel after wheel, no bumping, no tipping. The rails held their distance. Yet from up on the bridge, they still looked like they touched, way out at the edge of everything.

"So they never actually meet," Finnegan said slowly, "but they look like they do." He turned to her. "Fine, fine. You were right. I'm changing my vote."

Back inside, Norah marked one small dot on her paper and ran her road edges toward it. Kaelyn looked over and whistled. "Ooh, luminous," she said. "It's like the street is glowing."

"It's glowing because it finally makes sense," Norah said, and signed her name in the corner.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
Payton had taped the season schedule to the inside of her locker and put a red X on every loss, and by Friday there were six red Xs in a row, every single one from away games. The three wins, circled in green, had all happened in this gymnasium. She stared at the pattern during lunch, turning her milk carton slowly, until Jovan leaned over her shoulder.

"You're going to wear a hole in that paper," he said. "It's just bad luck."

"It's not luck," Payton said. "Every loss is on the road. Every win is here. That's not a coincidence, that's a rule." She flipped through her notebook, where she had copied the standings from the other divisions too. "Look at the volleyball teams. Same thing. Home teams win more than half their games on average. It's called home advantage. Evan told me he read it in a stats book, and it's everywhere, across a bunch of sports."

Jovan frowned at the numbers. "So we just can't win anywhere else? Should we abandon the season?"

"No. We need to figure out what's actually different and take it with us." The playoff seeding game was Monday, away, and if they lost it they would slide to the bottom bracket. Payton stood up so fast her tray rattled. "Practice. Now. Not in the gym, out on the blacktop, because that's what their court feels like. Different floor, different rims, buses instead of walking."

The coach agreed, barely, since the landlord who owned the rec center next door had lent them the outdoor hoops before and the keys were still in the office. Payton spent the whole hour on free throws with Evan rebounding for her, until the strange rim stopped feeling strange and started feeling just competent enough to trust. Evan, who had been sulking about the away losses all month, finally wiped his face with his shirt and said, "Okay. I take it back. This might actually work."

Monday, on the bus, Payton caught Jovan squeezing his eyes shut at every bump and handed him the last of her ginger candies without saying anything. He took it with a small nod.

The game stayed tied until the final minute, when Payton got fouled and stepped to the line on a rim she had shot at two hundred times on cold asphalt. She bounced the ball twice, just like practice, and let it go. The net barely moved. Jovan was already running to grab her before the second shot even dropped.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A meeting chair decides who speaks next and usually calls on someone who has not spoken yet before letting someone speak again.
story:
Abigail climbed onto the picnic table at the edge of the playground and slapped her notebook down. "Meeting of the Riverside Cleanup Club starts now!" Six kids turned toward her, and her heart did a little jump. Last week's meeting had been a disaster, and this week she had a plan: an agenda, written in her neatest handwriting, with "Petty the turtle" as item one, because someone had to speak up for the turtle trapped in the creek drain.

Last week's meeting flashed into her mind. Haylee had talked about the trash problem for ten straight minutes, and Ben had argued back the whole time, and the rest of the club had sat there with their hands up, waving, until everyone gave up and went home. Abigail had walked home furious and confused. There were six people in the club. So why had only two of them talked?

She rapped her pen against the table like a gavel. "First item. We need testimony about the creek. Who's actually seen trash in the water?" Hands shot up everywhere. Haylee's hand went up first, and Haylee started talking before Abigail could even nod at her. "I saw a chip bag and like forty soda cans and, oh, a bicycle wheel, and..."

"Haylee, hold on." Abigail's voice came out steadier than she felt. She had been thinking about this all week. When she'd watched the debate team practice through the gym window on Tuesday, she'd noticed something: the person running the meeting pointed at people. That person decided who spoke next. And the coach kept pointing at kids who hadn't spoken at all, not the ones who had already had a turn. The rule seemed to be that the chair calls on someone new before letting anyone speak again. She wasn't sure it would work, but she wanted to test it, right here, right now.

"Ben, you've seen the creek too, right? You spoke last week, so we'll come back to you." Ben opened his mouth, then shut it. She turned to the quiet kid in the green hoodie. "You first. What did you see?" He blinked, like he couldn't believe it, and then the words poured out of him: a shopping cart, a sandal, a nest made of plastic strips. Two more kids spoke after him. When Haylee raised her hand a second time, Abigail pointed at a girl who hadn't gone yet. "Haylee, you already had your turn, so she goes first."

Haylee frowned. "That's not fair, I'm the one who found the turtle."

"You'll get to talk. I'm the chair, and the chair picks who goes next." Abigail held her breath. For a second she thought Haylee might just stomp off, and the club would fall apart right there on the playground.

Then Haylee sat back down and raised her hand again, higher this time, like she was finally playing the game instead of fighting it. When her turn came, she stood up. "The turtle is stuck near the drain pipe and the water there smells impoverished, like, dead and empty. We need nets and buckets by Saturday." Abigail wrote "nets and buckets, Saturday" on the agenda and underlined it twice.

"Meeting's not over yet," Abigail said, grinning. "Who's never talked at one of our meetings before? You. Stand up. You're next."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Researchers usually define bullying as hurtful behavior that is repeated and involves an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals.
story:
Practice ended in forty minutes, and Luke had decided that before the scrimmage started, he would say something. For the third Tuesday in a row, a group of older boys had crowded around Aaryan while he tied his shoes, knocking his water bottle across the bench and calling him "Slow-mo" whenever Mr. Sok wasn't watching. The first time, Luke had told himself it was joking. The second time, he wasn't so sure. Now, watching Aaryan walk to the far end of the field alone, Luke counted the pattern in his head: three weeks, the same kids, the same target, and never once the other way around.

He thought about the fight he'd seen in the cafeteria last month, two seventh graders shouting at each other over a stolen fry, and how the vice principal had called it a one-time argument between equals. That had blown over in a day. This was different. It kept happening, and the older boys had size, numbers, and status on their side. His older sister had once read him a definition from a poster at her school, and now the pieces fit themselves together: hurtful behavior that is repeated and involves an imbalance of power. That was what bullying meant, not a single fight.

"You're doing the face," Makenna said, pulling her goggles off her head as she jogged over. The grass smelled like cut hay, and the evening sun made the goal net glow orange. "The thinking face."

"It's not joking anymore," Luke said. "It's bullying. It's repeated, and there's an imbalance of power." He said it quietly, testing it out loud, and it sounded right.

"Okay," Makenna said. "So what's the plan? If you charge in yelling, they'll just aim it at you too, and Aaryan gets nothing out of that." Luke nodded. Loud confrontation was fertile ground for a bigger mess. He needed something smaller. His mom had taken him for his flu vaccine that morning, and he remembered the nurse saying the tiny dose works better than the full illness. A small dose of standing up, then. He would recruit Aaryan himself as part of it, not just step in front of him like a shield.

The whistle blew for the scrimmage. Mr. Sok split the teams, and by luck or design, Aaryan ended up on Luke's side. When the older boys called "Slow-mo" from across the line, Luke didn't shout back. He jogged over to Aaryan and said, clearly enough to be heard, "Open on the left when you get the ball. I'll be there." Then he passed to Aaryan on the first possession, and again on the third, and Aaryan scored before the defenders caught up.

The twist came at the water break. One of the older boys, the tallest one, leaned over the fence near the fountain and muttered, "Nice shot, Slow-mo," but his voice had lost its edges, and he was already walking away before anyone could answer. Aaryan took a long drink, water running down his chin, and looked at Luke with his eyebrows up.

"Same time next Tuesday?" Aaryan asked, tossing him the ball.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
story:
Wyatt stood in Jaxton's kitchen with his tie knotted too tight and his dress shirt stiff as cardboard. "It's only a dance," Jaxton said, spiking his hair in the reflection of the toaster. "Two hours, then it's over." Wyatt knew that was true, but knowing didn't loosen the tie. "What if nobody dances with me? What if I just stand by the wall the whole time?" Jaxton's mom tried to console him from the stove, saying that even she had survived her first dance in 1998, which somehow made it worse, not better. On the counter sat a pizza Jaxton's dad had ordered, half of it covered in mushrooms. "I'm not eating fungus before the biggest night of my life," Jaxton said, and Wyatt laughed for the first time all afternoon.

The gym had been transformed with streamers, a snack table, and a mirror ball hanging from the ceiling on a long cord. One spotlight pointed at it from the corner, and the whole room swam with small moving spots of light. Wyatt did what he had feared: he stood by the wall. Katerina from his science class stood a few feet away, watching the spots sweep across the floor in slow curves.

"Have you figured out where they come from?" she asked. Wyatt looked up. The mirror ball turned slowly, and every tiny mirror tile on it caught the one spotlight beam and threw it somewhere different, so that a single light became hundreds of spots crawling over the walls, the bleachers, the dancers. He tracked one spot from the ceiling to the floor and back again. "Each little mirror," he said slowly, "takes the beam and sends it a different direction." He pointed at the ball, then traced a line with his finger down to a spot sliding across the basketball key. "So they're all coming from that one spotlight. Hundreds of them, from one."

"That's what I thought too," Katerina said. "So here's the thing. Watch the pattern." The spots weren't random. They swept in long slow rows, then doubled back, following the ball as it turned. "If you know where a row is going," she said, "you can be standing in it when it arrives." She stepped out onto the floor, waited, and a stripe of light crossed her shoes just as she'd predicted. Wyatt laughed out loud. It was like the room itself was playing a game with them, and the game had rules he could learn.

"Okay," he said, and loosened his tie one notch. "Then dancing is just moving to where the light is going to be." It was a temporary theory, he knew, and probably a silly one, but it gave his feet somewhere to go. He stepped out beside Katerina and Jaxton, and when the next row of spots swept past, all three of them were standing inside it, glittering from head to shoes. "Fungus power," Jaxton called over the music, pointing at his shoes. "Look at that."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
story:
