The school bus wasn't going anywhere, which was the whole point. Mr. Sánchez had organized a "Bee on the Bus" as practice for regionals, and thirty kids were squeezed into the seats while the driver, who apparently lost a bet, sat up front eating sunflower seeds like a judge at a popcorn festival.

"Round three," Mr. Sánchez announced from the front, holding his clipboard like a golden ticket. "Aaron, your word is vaccine."

Aaron stood up so fast he banged his elbow on the window. "Vaccine. V-A-C..." He stopped. His brain did that awful freeze, the one where the letters swim like minnows. He was pretty sure it wasn't a C after the A. He was pretty sure it was an S.

"Take your time," said Chantelle from two rows back, grinning. She'd already survived "commute" in round one by spelling it slowly, like she was defusing a bomb.

Aaron remembered something the regional rules sheet had said, something he'd skimmed while eating cereal that morning. It had seemed trivial then. Now it felt like the most important sentence ever printed. He pieced it together: a speller could start the word over. But if he started over and changed any letter he'd already said, that counted as a misspelling. So if he said V-A-C and then went V-A-S, the bell would ding and he'd be out, no arguing.

Which meant one thing. If V-A-C was wrong, he was already sunk. If it was right, saying it again exactly the same way was safe. He had to test it without changing a single letter.

"V-A-C," he said again, carefully, like stepping on ice. "C-I-N-E. Vaccine."

Mr. Sánchez consulted his clipboard. "Correct."

The back rows burst into applause. Brooklyn, who'd been eliminated on "rhythm" and was still bitter about it, stood on her seat and shouted, "He restarted! Is that legal? I want a recount!"

Mr. Sánchez held up both hands. "He started over, which is allowed. If he had changed any letter he'd already said, it would have counted as a misspelling. He didn't change anything." He turned to Aaron. "Nice recovery."

Chantelle leaned into the aisle. "How did you know you could do that?"

"I didn't, exactly," Aaron admitted. "I just knew I couldn't fix a letter once I'd said it. So I figured the only safe move was to say the same letters over again and pray the first one was right."

"That's the most Aaron plan I've ever heard," said Brooklyn, hopping down from her seat.

Round four began, and the bus windows fogged up from all the breathing. Chantelle got "labrador" and spelled it like a champion. Aaron got "parallel," sweat through both Rs, and survived by one careful letter.

Then it was down to him and Chantelle, alone in the front seats while everyone else crowded behind them like it was the World Cup. Mr. Sánchez looked at his list and smiled.

"Final word. Aaron, your word is scissors."

Aaron closed his eyes. Somewhere in the dark, S-C came floating up, followed by that treacherous middle where anything could hide.

"S-C-I-S-S," he began, and heard Chantelle whisper, "Oh, he's got this."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
story:
Clara stood in her aunt's crowded living room holding a photograph of her grandmother and a paper bag full of marigolds, and she had no idea what to do with either one. Every table had been pushed against the walls, and in the corner stood a wooden table draped with a purple cloth, already stacked with candles, pan dulce, and a small clay skeleton wearing tiny glasses exactly like the ones her grandmother had worn. Cousins everywhere, aunts calling out from the kitchen, and her friend Tyrell from next door hovering near the door with his jacket still on because he had never been to anything like this before.

"Is this a funeral?" Tyrell whispered.

"No," said Clara. "It's Dia de los Muertos. It happens on November first and second, and families build altars. My tía called them ofrendas on the phone." She frowned at the table, then at the bag of marigolds in her hand, bright orange as traffic cones. "What I don't understand is where the flowers go. Everyone kept saying they matter, but nobody said what to actually do with them."

Clementine, Clara's cousin, appeared at her elbow with a plan of her own. "I want the photo in my bedroom after tonight," she announced. "I asked first. Grandma lived with us before she moved in with you, so it's fair." Clara gripped the frame tighter. She had a different want, though she couldn't have named it yet. She only knew that tonight the photo belonged somewhere specific, if she could figure out where.

While the aunts argued over whether the pan dulce was placed the conventional way or upside down, Clara studied the altar. She noticed the candles made a scent, the bread made a scent, and the marigolds, when she opened the bag, made the strongest scent of all. On the phone, her tía had said the color and scent guide the spirits home. Home. Clara turned the word over. Not just to the table. To the house. From wherever you started, all the way here. "Tyrell," she said slowly, "if the flowers guide her, shouldn't there be flowers from the front door to the altar? Like a runway?"

Tyrell looked at the door, then the altar, and his face did the thing it did when a math problem suddenly made sense. "A path," he said. "That's testable."

So they tested it. Clara set her grandmother's photograph carefully on the ofrenda between the candles, and then she and Tyrell and, after some negotiation, Clementine too, knelt in the hallway and scattered marigold petals in a loose orange line, from the front door, past the kitchen where the tamales steamed, all the way to the corner table. Clara found herself wondering as she worked: if Grandma's spirit really did walk in tonight, would she come through the petal path, or drift in some other way Clara couldn't see? There was no way to know for sure. That was the strange, shivery part. But testing it made the not-knowing feel like a door left open on purpose.

Clementine watched the last petals settle. She had been quiet for a while, which for Clementine was a long time. "Maybe the photo should stay on the ofrenda," she said at last. "Not in my room. Not just at my house. It belongs here, where she can find it every year." Clara set the frame down beside the little skeleton with the tiny glasses, and Clementine straightened it, just so.

Later, when the candles were lit and the room smelled of marigolds and cinnamon, Clara stood with her parents at the end of the orange path. Tomorrow was only November second, so there was still another whole day, but tonight she leaned close to her grandmother's face in the photograph and whispered, "Follow the flowers. They go all the way to you."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: In South Asia, crops sown at the start of the summer monsoon and harvested in autumn are called kharif crops, and rice is the main one.
story:
The trail climbed through pines before it dropped toward the creek, and John kept one hand on his water bottle and the other on the crumpled page in his pocket. On the page was the quiz question Mr. Sánchez had written on the board that morning: explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia. John had until Monday, and he did not have an answer yet. Angel walked ahead of him, kicking a pinecone, and Annabel kept stopping to look at things, which was her way of hiking.

"Everything's about heat," Angel said when John read the question out loud. "That's my whole answer. It gets hot, it rains. Done."

"That's not an answer," Annabel said. "That's a shrug with words."

John thought about his grandfather, who had farmed a small field in Punjab before moving here. Every summer he told the same story about waiting through weeks of dry heat while everyone watched the sky, and then, when the first big rains came, the whole village went out and planted rice in the mud. "Those are kharif crops," his grandfather always said, "sown at the start of the summer monsoon, harvested in autumn." Rice first, always rice, because rice needed all that water.

They stopped at the creek for lunch. Mr. Sánchez, who had hiked ahead, was sitting on a flat rock with a tin cup, watching the water slide past. John crouched at the edge and put his fingers in. Cold. Then he pressed his palm flat against the sun-baked rock beside the creek. Hot enough to pull back from.

"The water's cold and the land is burning," John said slowly. He was building an inference, piece by piece, the way his grandfather stacked bricks. Land heats faster than water, and all summer South Asia is a huge hot land next to a cooler ocean. Hot air rises, so the cooler, wet ocean air has to flow in to take its place, and when that wet air rises over the land, it dumps its water. That is the monsoon. "It's like the land is inhaling," he said. "All summer it breathes in the ocean."

"You could test it," Annabel said. She found a shallow puddle in the sun and a dry patch of dirt beside it, laid her hand on each, and frowned. "The dirt's hotter. Same sun."

"That's the test," John said. "Small version of a whole continent."

On the walk back, Mr. Sánchez pointed at a gray shape ambling up a dead tree, an owl settling into a hole. "Nocturnal," he said. "Heading to bed while we head home." John laughed, then went quiet, working the sentence he would say on Monday: the land heats, the ocean air flows in, the rains arrive, and the rice goes into the ground at the very first storm, kharif crops, harvested in autumn.

"Monday," Angel said, "you talk, I nod."

"Angel," John said, "you're my chart paper."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Sprinting the first lap faster than a pace you can hold uses up quick anaerobic energy early, so the runner usually slows sharply on the second lap.
story:
At the first track practice of the season, Kayla's coach handed her a stopwatch and a clipboard, telling her to document the lap times of everyone trying out for the eight hundred metres. Kayla stood at the fence near the finish line, clicking the button each time a runner went past. When Valentina blew by on the first lap, fifteen seconds ahead of everyone else, Kayla wrote down 68 seconds and thought, that girl has this race won already.

She was wrong. On the second lap Valentina's stride shortened, her arms dropped, and runners she had left behind began to stream past her on the final straight. Her second lap came in at 96 seconds, nearly half a minute slower, and she crossed the line eighth, gasping with her hands on her knees. Kayla stared at the two numbers on her clipboard. It wasn't just that Valentina was tired. Everyone was tired at the end. Valentina had slowed down sharply, like a car running out of fuel, while Kamila, who had run her first lap in a steady 80 seconds, had come through her second lap in 82 and finished third.

That night Kayla spread her clipboard notes across the kitchen table like evidence from a case. Every runner who had gone out fast had faded badly. Every runner who had held an even pace had passed people at the end. She didn't know exactly why the fast starters fell apart, but the pattern was there, plain as footprints in snow on the tundra, impossible to miss once you looked. She decided to test it herself the next practice, even though it would mean letting Valentina pull far ahead of her in front of everybody.

The next afternoon, Valentina sprinted away from the line as if the race were two hundred metres, not eight hundred. Kayla counted her own steps and held back, letting the gap widen until Valentina was half the straight ahead. Her legs burned with wanting to chase. Kamila, running beside her, panted, "She's gone, Kayla."

"She'll come back," Kayla said, and kept her pace.

At the bell for the final lap, Kayla still felt strong, her breathing deep instead of ragged. Valentina's shoulders were already sagging on the back curve. Kayla passed her on the final straight with plenty left, then leaned at the line and looked at the stopwatch on her own wrist. Eighty seconds, then eighty-one. She walked a slow cool-down lap, found Valentina sitting against the fence, and held out the clipboard. "Look. First lap versus second lap, for everyone." Valentina took it and studied the columns for a long moment. "So the trick," she said slowly, "is not going faster than you can hold." Kayla nodded and clicked the stopwatch to zero.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person often also chants the haftarah, a reading from the books of the Prophets.
story:
Ellie had chosen the cemetery because nobody there would interrupt her, and because her grandmother, who was buried under the oak near the gate, had been the one who read Torah every year at her synagogue until her hands got too stiff. Ellie spread her binder of Hebrew text on the flat top of a stone bench, adjusted her sweatshirt against the October wind, and started chanting her Torah portion for the eleventh time that week.

She got through four lines before she forgot the melody on the fifth and had to start over. The grass around her was sparse, brown patches mixed with green, and a crow was watching her from the fence as if it had opinions. "Don't judge me," she told it. The crow did not answer, which was probably a compromise on its part.

"You're going to freeze out here." Miko came up the path with two hot chocolates in foam cups and her scarf wound up to her chin. "My mom saw you cut through our yard. She says hi, and also wear a hat."

"I can't practice at home. Every time I mess up, my brother makes that buzzer sound." Ellie took a cup anyway. "At least here the audience is quiet."

Miko sat down on the bench and flipped through Ellie's binder, because she had no sense of personal property. "Okay, so this is your Torah reading, right? The one from Genesis." She kept flipping. "Then what's this other thing? It says H-A-F..."

Ellie grabbed the binder back. Her stomach did something strange, like a drawer sliding open in a dark room she hadn't looked in. "That's not mine. That's leftover from the girl who had her bat mitzvah before me." She looked at the cover page again. The date on it was hers. The name was hers.

"What is it, though?" Miko asked.

Ellie stared at the Hebrew, which was definitely not from Genesis. "It's a haftarah," she said slowly. "It comes from the books of the Prophets. You chant it too." She had heard the word before, sitting in services, drifting past her the way words do when you assume they belong to other people's families. Apparently it belonged to hers now. She had been preparing for weeks as if she had one reading to learn, and she had two.

For a moment she felt something close to despair, the kind that makes you want to lie down on a cold bench forever. Then she remembered her grandmother, who had decided at Ellie's age that she wanted to read Torah even though the rabbi at the time said girls didn't. Her grandmother had learned anyway, walking to the synagogue library every afternoon after school, because apparently stubbornness ran in the family like a plumbing problem.

"Okay," Ellie said out loud. "Eleven weeks. If I do the Torah portion in the mornings and the haftarah after school, that's maybe eight lines a day." She was already writing numbers in the margin, which Miko watched with the respect one gives a person defusing a bomb.

"You know," Miko said, "most people would just cry."

"I cried on Tuesday. Today I'm making a schedule." Ellie squared her shoulders, took a breath, and began to chant the strange new lines into the wind, while the crow, unimpressed, flew off over her grandmother's oak.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, if the door stays closed.
story:
Florence was in the backyard trying to finish her model windmill when every light in the house went dark at once. The porch lamp died, the hum of the refrigerator stopped, and the whole street went quiet in a way that made her look up. Her father came out with a torch and said the power company reported a fault that might take a day or two to repair. A day or two. Florence set down her windmill and thought immediately of the freezer in the garage, because that week it happened to be only half full, with the big shop still four days away.

"We should move things to Keon's house," she said. "His power comes from a different grid, doesn't it?" Her father shook his head. "Same grid, I'm afraid. Half the neighbourhood is out." Florence chewed her lip. She remembered something Mr. Sutton had mentioned at the school's agriculture club, of all places, when they were talking about how farmers store harvests. He had said a full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, as long as the door stays closed. Nobody had written it down, but Florence had, in the back of her project notebook, because it sounded like the kind of thing that might matter someday.

She fetched the notebook from her room by torchlight and found the page. Then she did the arithmetic out loud. "It's only half full, so we've got about 24 hours, not 48. And the repair is a day or two. So if it takes longer than one day, the food's in trouble." Her father frowned at the freezer door as if it were already leaking cold. "So what do we do?" Florence held up a hand, thinking. "We don't open it. Not even once. And we fill the empty half with something, because the rule says a full one lasts 48 hours."

They worked fast before any more cold could creep out. Florence gathered bottles from the recycling bin while her father fetched jugs from the tap, and they packed the empty shelf of the freezer so tightly that it felt like a proper full one again. Then they taped a note to the door that said DO NOT OPEN, and Kabir, who had climbed over the back fence to see why the street was dark, added a drawing of a snarling snowman to make the warning feel more authentic. They ate dinner in the backyard by torchlight, and Florence checked the freezer timer she had set on her watch, just to keep track of the hours.

The twist came at ten the next morning, when the power came back on, barely twelve hours into the danger zone. The lights blinked awake, the refrigerator began to hum, and Florence ran to the garage and put her hand near the freezer seal. Still cold, still safe. But when she opened it to return the bottles to the recycling, she noticed something she had not packed: her mother's bag of frozen peas from last month, buried at the back, half-thawed and refrozen into a lump shaped exactly like the windmill Florence had been building. "Well," she said, holding it up to the light, "at least now we know it was shut the whole time." Her father laughed, and Kabir, still in the yard, called out, "Can I have the pea windmill?"

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: If prices rise faster than a savings account's interest rate, the money in the account buys less each year even though the balance grows.
story:
Grayson sat at the kitchen table with a letter from the bank, a pencil, and the last of the hot chocolate going lukewarm in his mug. The letter said his savings account had earned compound interest for five years. He could hear the furnace humming below, working to insulate the house against the February cold, and somewhere upstairs his little brother was arguing with a sock.

Five years ago, when he was seven, he had put two hundred dollars into the account. It was birthday money and lemonade-stand money, saved for one thing: the blue bike at Mr. Saleh's shop down the street. Back then the bike cost two hundred dollars. The bank letter said his balance was now two hundred and twenty dollars, because the compound interest earned interest on the interest each year. Grayson had learned a technique in math class for checking this: draw a table, one row per year, and watch the balance climb a little more each time. He tried it with simple interest too, where the interest is only ever calculated on the original two hundred, and he saw that compound gave him a few extra dollars over the five years. Compound won. He felt pleased with himself, so pleased that he put on his boots and walked to Mr. Saleh's shop in the thin afternoon light, his breath hanging in the air.

The blue bike still hung in the window. The tag on it said two hundred and sixty dollars.

"How long has it been two sixty?" Grayson asked.

Mr. Saleh rubbed the tag with his thumb. "Prices have gone up most years since you started staring through my window, Grayson. Small bites, but they add up."

Grayson walked home slowly, doing the arithmetic in his head. His money had grown from two hundred to two hundred and twenty. The bike had grown from two hundred to two hundred and sixty. The account balance had gone up every single year, and yet it covered less of the bike now than it had when he was seven, because the price had climbed faster than the interest. He tested the idea the only way he could think of: he wrote the two numbers on the back of the bank letter and drew an arrow from one to the other, just to see the gap.

At home he texted Simona, because she was the one person he knew who kept a spreadsheet of everything.

"Did you know money can grow and shrink at the same time?" he typed. "The number gets bigger but it buys less. My two twenty is now forty short of the bike."

She replied with a single line: "So the account's growing slower than the prices. That's the whole trick of it."

Grayson set his phone down beside the letter and looked at the blue bike through his bedroom window, still visible two blocks away in Mr. Saleh's bright shopfront glass. Then he pulled his snow shovel out of the closet and set it by the door, where he would see it in the morning.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
story:
The cutting board skidded again, and Emilia's knife hand jumped back before the blade even touched the onion. "Okay," she said, staring at the board like it had personally insulted her. "Why does it only slide when I press down?"

Graydon leaned over the camp stove, where his pot of water was starting to grumble. "Maybe the counter's slanted."

Emilia crouched until her eyes were level with the bench. "It's not. Look, it's flat." She pressed the board with her palm. It stayed put. Then she mimicked a chop, pushing down and slightly forward, and the board shot toward Aedan like a hockey puck. "There! It moves when I cut. Something about the cutting makes it slide."

"That's a problem," Aedan said, peeling their third onion with the focus of someone defusing a bomb. "Mr. Otieno said if anyone bleeds, nobody gets pasta sauce."

"The sauce is crucial," Graydon agreed solemnly. "It's the whole reason we volunteered to cook tonight instead of washing dishes."

Mr. Otieno had already wandered off toward the fire pit, so Emilia was on her own. She thought about her grandmother's kitchen at home, trying to picture the counter there. Had the board ever slid? She couldn't remember it happening once. But her grandmother did something before she started, some little ritual Emilia had watched a hundred times without really seeing. A cloth. She ran a cloth under the tap and wrung it out and laid it flat under the board. Was that it, or was it just habit?

Only one way to find out. She dunked a dish towel in the water jug, wrung it until it stopped dripping, and spread it on the bench. "Watch this," she said, and set the board on top.

"Wait," Aedan said. "What's the towel for?"

"I'm testing an idea." She curled her left hand into the claw Mr. Otieno had shown them that morning, fingertips tucked in, knuckles guiding the blade, and chopped. Down, down, down. The board didn't move a millimeter. She chopped faster, half the onion dissolving into neat little pieces, and still it held steady. "It works! A damp towel under the board stops it from sliding while you chop."

Graydon abandoned his pot to press on her board with both hands. "It's stuck there like it's glued."

"It's not glue, it's just wet," Emilia said, though honestly she wasn't sure of the difference in this case, and that wondering felt like the good kind, the kind worth chewing on later.

Aedan migrated down the bench to Emilia's end, dragging the onion bin. "Teach me the claw," they said. "And the towel thing. But mostly the claw, because I value my fingers."

"Knuckles forward, fingertips back, like a bear paw," Emilia said, guiding the knife. "The blade rests on your knuckle and can't get to anything important."

By the time Mr. Otieno came back to check on them, the onions were golden in the pan, garlic hissing, and the whole picnic table smelled like an actual Italian kitchen instead of a campsite. He raised his eyebrows at the damp towel peeking out from under her board.

"Nice," he said. "Who taught you that?"

"Nobody," Emilia said. "I watched my grandmother do it for years, and today the board kept escaping, so I finally figured out what the towel was for."

"Huh," said Mr. Otieno. "Some things you learn by being told. Some things you learn by chasing a cutting board across a bench."

"Some things you learn by almost losing a thumb," Aedan said, holding up all ten fingers in triumph.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: In a pick and roll, after setting the screen, the screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler.
story:
Connor stood at the top of the key on the cracked court at Riverside Park, bouncing the ball and wondering why nobody was ever open. Zack waved both arms at the far sideline, smothered by a defender. Elianne was supposed to set a screen for him, and she did, planting herself beside Connor's defender like a fence. But every time Connor dribbled past her, the defender just switched onto him, and Elianne stood there watching, flat-footed. Something hidden was going wrong, and Connor wanted to find it.

"Try it again," he said, "but this time watch what my defender does." He dribbled off Elianne's screen and looked back. His defender slid over to him, sure, but Elianne's defender came with her and stayed glued on. He noticed something else, too: for half a second, the lane to the basket was empty. Was it empty because Elianne wasn't in it? He chewed on the question while Zack jogged over, breathing hard.

"You look like you're solving a math problem," Zack said. "Basketball is not math."

"Kind of it is," Connor said. He pulled out his phone and typed a message to Mr. Li, who coached the rec league and answered his texts faster than anyone's actual dad: "When Elianne screens for me and just stands there, nobody gets open. Is she supposed to do something after?" The reply buzzed back within a minute. "After setting the screen, the screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler. Look it up, it's called the pick and roll." Connor read it twice. "That's it," he said. "Elianne, you're not a statue. You're a door that swings."

Elianne frowned. "A door that swings?"

"After you screen me, you roll to the hoop," Connor said. "My defender has to choose, and either way somebody's open."

They ran it once, and Elianne turned too late. They ran it again, and her defender hesitated, caught between two jobs like a parasite that couldn't decide which host to cling to, and Elianne cut hard toward the basket with her hands up. Connor fired the bounce pass between two defenders. Elianne caught it and laid it off the backboard and in.

Zack pointed at them with a look of sinister delight, as if they had invented something forbidden. "Okay, that was actually beautiful. Do it again, and this time I'll space out to the corner and collaborate."

Connor backed out to the top of the key, spun the ball in his hands, and called it: "Elly, screen and roll. Zack, corner. Go."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
Hayden sat in the waiting room of Dr. Okafor's office, folding the corner of his intake form into smaller and smaller triangles. His mom had made the appointment because his stomach hurt before every math test this semester, always in the same spot, always vanishing by lunch. He wanted an answer, even a boring one, and he wanted it before Friday's quiz.

"Hayden?" A girl from his grade, Allyson, sat two chairs down with a violin case balanced on her knees. "What are you doing here?"

"Stomachaches. You?"

"Twisted my wrist at practice. I have a recital Saturday." Her knee was bouncing, and her eyes kept flicking to the clock, the door, the clock again. Hayden noticed she was also, without looking, keeping perfect track of her case, her paperwork, and her phone sliding off her knee. She caught it every time before it fell.

"That's weird," he said. "You're jittery but you're not dropping anything."

"My coach says stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can actually help you focus, like right before a race." She shrugged. "So I'm trying to believe her."

The nurse called "Allyson?" and Hayden watched her stand, square her shoulders, and walk through the door like someone stepping onto a stage. It gave him an idea. His stomach hurt before tests, yes. But he had never once frozen during one. When the nerves compress his whole attention down to the paper in front of him, he actually got more done, not less. Maybe the pain wasn't the problem itself. Maybe it was a signal, and he had been reading it as damage.

When it was his turn, Dr. Okafor pressed gently on his stomach, asked about sleep and food, and said nothing was wrong with his gut. Then she asked a question he hadn't expected. "What's happening in your life when it hurts?"

"Tests. Anxiety, I guess. Before, not during." He told her about Allyson and her recital, and her coach's line about short bursts. Dr. Okafor nodded slowly.

"So your stress shows up early, like an alarm that rings too loud but at the right time," she said. "We can work on coping, breathing techniques, ways to turn the volume down. And you can practice telling people when it's too much. Even with your mom. Boundaries around study time, maybe."

"The volume down," Hayden repeated. "Not off."

"Exactly."

On the drive home, he tried her breathing pattern, four counts in, six out, his hand flat on the middle-school-fundamental geometry flashcards in his lap. His stomach still twinged. But when his mom asked how it went, he said, "I have a plan," and turned the first card over.

"Obtuse angle," he read, and the word settled in his mind, sharp and clear as anything.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
story:
The yellow shirt went into the laundry basket before anyone could see the dark rings under the arms. Hannah stared at the basket for a moment, then pulled the shirt back out and held it at arm's length, sniffing. It smelled like the change room after gym, and that was a problem, because in two days she had to stand up in front of her science class and present her wind turbine project, arms raised, turning the model blades for everyone to see.

Last week had been worse, though. She flashed back to it now: Mr. Saleh calling her to the board to label the parts of the water cycle, and Aikam sliding his chair sideways, just an inch, and turning his face toward the window. He had not said anything. He had not needed to. She had kept her arms glued to her sides for the rest of the period, and even Roxane's folded note, "you okay?", had only made her cheeks hotter.

In the bathroom she found the stick her mom kept beside the sink. She twisted it up and swiped it on, then checked the label while it dried. It said deodorant in looping green letters, with the word natural underneath, and farther down, in smaller print: reduces odor. She read it twice. It did not say anything about sweat. She texted Roxane: "is your thing deodorant or antiperspirant? what's the difference?"

Roxane's reply came fast. "my mom got me antiperspirant. it says it plugs the sweat ducts so you don't sweat. deodorant doesn't stop sweat, it just covers the smell." Hannah stood in the hallway holding the phone, thinking it through. That explained a lot. Last month, before she had borrowed anything, she had sweated straight through her shirt with no smell at all, because she had used nothing. This week she had used her mom's stick, and she still sweated, just pleasantly pine-scented, which was not exactly the victory it sounded like. The yellow shirt, still in her hand, proved it.

She carried the shirt downstairs, where her mom was supervising a pot of soup that had begun to spit. "Can we go to the store?" Hannah asked, and when her mom raised an eyebrow at the bundle under her arm, Hannah just said, "I need the one that plugs the ducts. Roxane explained it." Her mom turned down the burner, looked at her for a long second, and then reached for her keys.

At the store Hannah read every label in the aisle until she found it: antiperspirant and deodorant together in one stick, in plain white. Her mom set it on the counter and added something else, a wrapped package she kept turned away. When they got home, Hannah found it waiting on her bed: the yellow shirt, washed and folded, with a card that read, "For the turbine presentation. Knock them over. Love, Mom." It was, Hannah decided, the most authentic get-well card ever written for a shirt, and she laughed so hard she had to sit down.

Two days later she stood in front of the class, raised both arms to spin the blades of the turbine, and heard the tiny generator whir. Her underarms stayed dry. She caught Roxane's eye at the back and flashed her a grin, and Aikam gave her a thumbs up without sliding his chair anywhere at all.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
story:
Mila popped the last bag of chips open at the picnic table by the soccer fields, where the end-of-season party was already going weird. Half her teammates were laughing at Bryson's impression of the referee, and the other half stood around like statues holding paper cups. "Why does everyone look like we lost the championship?" Mila asked Ellia. "We won it. Sort of. We came fourth."

"Because next year the rec league splits us up," Ellia said. "Different teams, different coaches. This team won't exist." She sighed into her cup like it was a tiny microphone.

That was the strange part, Mila thought. Nobody was sad about losing games. They were sad about the team itself ending, which was a thing you couldn't see or kick. On the walk to the park she had listened to her older sister's psychology tutor rambling on about group stages, and one word had stuck in her head: adjourning. The tutor had said that in 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. Mila had tuned out the rest because the tutor also kept saying "storming" and "norming" like a pirate. But now the word felt useful.

She decided to test it. "Hey, Bryson," she called. "Pretend this is a practice. Just for a minute."

Bryson perked up immediately, because Bryson would simulate a fire drill if you asked him to. He blew a whistle that he did not own, yelled "Two lines, ladder drills!" and suddenly the whole team was sprinting between cones somebody had left in the grass, wheezing and giggling. The statue half of the party came alive. When they collapsed back at the table, Mr. Hassan, who coached the team, raised an eyebrow at the trampled grass.

"Interesting strategy," he said. "You made yourselves miserable on purpose."

"It's a science experiment," Mila said. "Our tutor says groups go through stages, and the last one is adjourning. That's when a group finishes its work and breaks up. In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added it." She shrugged. "So this sad feeling is normal. It has a name."

Ellia squinted. "So if it has a name, is there a cure?"

"I'm working on the cure," Mila said. She pulled out her phone and opened the group chat, which was named GOATLLAMAS for reasons nobody remembered. "What if we keep the chat going next year? Different teams, same chat. It's like the team keeps existing but in a phone."

"That's not equivalent to a real team," Ellia said. "You can't head a chat into a goal."

"You'd be surprised," said Bryson, who had already sent eleven llama stickers.

Mr. Hassan laughed so hard he nearly dropped the trophy, the small plastic one for fourth place that Mila had secretly decided was as good as gold. She held it up over the table like a championship cup. "Same time next summer," she announced. "Everybody here. I'll bring the cones."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
story:
Sarah had practiced the sonata eleven times that week, and every time the same thing went wrong. The music slowed beautifully at the ritardando, the way Mr. Mehta had marked it, but then she kept crawling along at that slow speed until the final notes, and it sounded wrong, like a river turning to mud.

"You're doing it again," Pyper said from the doorway of the practice room. She had come early for the recital and sat down to listen. "The middle part sounds great, but the ending drags."

"The ending is supposed to be fast," Sarah said, staring at the page. "It's supposed to be exciting. I don't know why it won't come back."

She looked at the measure after the rit. There was a marking she had been skating past for weeks, two small words printed above the staff: "a tempo." She had assumed it was some leftover instruction, maybe telling her to keep the tempo she already had. But if that were true, why would the composer write anything at all?

"Wait," she said, and put her hands back on the keys. "Maybe it's telling me something. Maybe it means go back to the original speed."

Pyper leaned over the score. "Try it. Right now, before you generate another excuse."

Sarah played the passage again. She let the rit. slow the phrase down, and at the "a tempo" she pushed forward, back to the speed the piece had started with. The ending leapt out of the keyboard, bright and rushing, and the last chord rang through the empty hall like a door slamming open. Her hands stayed on the keys, and she felt her heart going almost as fast as the sixteenth notes had.

"That's it," Pyper said. "That's the piece. That's the whole piece."

Mr. Mehta found them in the practice room ten minutes later, tuning the piano lamp and stacking programs for the evening audience. "Sarah, I heard that run-through from the lobby. Something changed."

She showed him the two small words and told him her idea, and he nodded once, the way he did when a student found something on her own. "Play it that way tonight," he said. "Play it exactly that way."

When her turn came, she walked out past the dark rows of seats, and the lights on the piano were warm and arid on her hands. She set the program on the rack, found the first measure, and began. The ritardando arrived like a held breath, and then, at the two small words, she released it and let the ending run. From the second row, Pyper cupped her hands around her mouth and whispered, "A tempo!"

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: Excel's 'Show Values As' option can display each count as a percentage of its column or row total, so grades with different numbers of students can be compared fairly.
story:
Addison sat cross-legged on Harnoor's bedroom floor with a laptop balanced on a binder, glaring at a spreadsheet full of survey answers. Harnoor had convinced half the school to fill out a questionnaire about the spring dance theme, and now three hundred rows of answers stared back at them.

"We need this done by Friday," Harnoor said, sliding a mug of hot chocolate next to the laptop. "Mr. Bui said the student council has to present real numbers, not just vibes."

"I know, I know." Addison highlighted the column of grade levels and the column of theme choices. "Mr. Bui showed us pivot tables last week. You drag the grades into the rows, the theme into the columns, and it counts everything for you." She built it in two minutes: rows for grades six, seven, and eight, columns for each theme. Space Carnival won every single question. Grade six liked it best, grade seven liked it best, grade eight liked it best.

"That's it then," Harnoor said. "Space Carnival. Done by Thursday, even." But Addison kept staring at the counts. Grade eight had a huge number, one hundred and ten responses, while grade six had only forty. "Wait," she said slowly. "The eighth graders didn't win because they like Space Carnival more. There are just way more of them answering. It's like when my cousin said his family boycotts a certain cereal brand, so obviously the store sold less of it. It wasn't because everyone hated it. It was because his family has nine kids." She clicked into the pivot table options, hunting through the menus until she found something called "Show Values As." A list dropped down, and she chose the option that turned each count into a percentage of its column total.

The table reshaped itself. Space Carnival dropped to second place in grade six, behind Movie Night, and in grade seven the two themes were nearly tied. Only grade eight still loved Space Carnival best. "There," Addison said. "Now it's fair. Every grade gets compared out of one hundred, no matter how many kids answered."

Harnoor leaned over her shoulder, then grabbed a sticky note and wrote "Movie Night, grade six, 41 percent" at the top. "I was pessimistic about finishing tonight," she admitted. "I thought we'd be here until midnight."

"We still have to make the chart look good," Addison said. She dragged Movie Night to the front of the table and watched the columns rearrange. "And tomorrow we tell Mr. Bui that grade eight has been voting like a giant family of nine kids."
